title: China Weighs Blocking Exports of Its Own AI Models and Chips, Mirroring US Curbs
subhead: Beijing regulators are considering placing Chinese-built AI models and accelerators under an export licensing regime for the first time, a shift as notable as anything Washington has done in the chip war.

sections.heading: China Considers Export Controls on Its Own AI Models and Chips
sections.body:
Chinese regulators are weighing tighter export controls on home-grown artificial intelligence models and the chips that run them, according to the Financial Times, citing two people involved in the discussions. The commerce ministry has been consulting leading domestic AI and chip groups about possible safeguards; nothing has been finalized and no draft has been published, the FT stresses.

The move would extend Beijing's technology defenses well beyond raw materials. Officials are reportedly reviewing export lists covering AI- and chip-related goods, clarifying licence criteria, tightening end-user checks, and raising hurdles for transferring technology abroad — with the stated aim of keeping China's most advanced systems and fastest-growing startups from being acquired by the West.

The groundwork was laid earlier this month. Reuters reported the commerce ministry held talks with Alibaba, ByteDance and the startup Z.ai about limiting overseas access to flagship systems including Alibaba's Qwen, ByteDance's Doubao and Z.ai's GLM-5.2, covering both closed and open-weight models and floating a tiered review under which frontier systems could stay at home entirely.

The chip element is the newer part of the picture: folding finished AI accelerators and the models trained on them into a formal licensing regime would be a marked shift in how Beijing wields industrial policy. Officials have stressed to Reuters curbs might apply only to future models, and Beijing rarely telegraphs export policy before it lands.
sections.whyItMatters: This would be the mirror image of US policy — China treating its best AI as a protected strategic asset rather than something to share. It could fragment the global open-model ecosystem just as firms like Nvidia race to lock in open-source AI.

sections.heading: US and China Arm for Conflict in Orbit
sections.body:
A Reuters analysis (Sept 2) details how Washington and Beijing are preparing for warfare in space. In June, a secretive unmanned Chinese spaceplane closely monitored by US military analysts released a small satellite in an orbital region crowded with commercial and military satellites — an episode analysts read as practice for deploying 'hunter-killer' systems capable of tailing and disabling adversary spacecraft.

Both sides are fielding orbital weapons platforms and ISR constellations. An Asia Times piece argues the opening moves of a future US-China conflict over Taiwan could unfold hundreds of kilometers above the Pacific rather than across it, as both forces race to seize the high ground in orbit. Separately, China has formally unveiled a 30-satellite 'Cislunar CubeSat Constellation' to provide persistent space-weather monitoring across Earth-Moon space by 2030 — billed (per MSN/space reporting) as the only announced cislunar radiation monitoring network on track before crewed lunar missions begin — alongside a multilateral Earth-Moon cube-sat science program involving institutions from Thailand and elsewhere.
sections.whyItMatters: Orbit is becoming a contested domain before rules of the road exist. China pairing civilian lunar-monitoring constellations with demonstrated orbital-maneuver capability widens its lead in both commercial and military space infrastructure.

sections.heading: Nickel and Chip-Grade Minerals Become a Point of Contention
sections.body:
Indonesia is tightening state control over the world's largest nickel supply just as China pushes back. Per Asahi Shimbun, Jakarta is restricting the metal after years of betting it would anchor a homegrown EV industry and as global demand shifts away from heavy nickel reliance. Reuters and Business Times report Chinese-controlled Indonesian smelters are weighing coordinated output cuts on weak prices — and that Beijing has sent an unusually blunt diplomatic message to Jakarta. A Financial Times report (cited by MSN) says China issued a warning tied to billions in Indonesian nickel commitments as the economic escalation across the EV supply chain deepens.

Separately, Asia Times reports the US and Japan are racing to build a new chip-grade critical-minerals supply chain as China curbs exports — but that geopolitical disputes among allies are slowing the effort. July customs data show China's strategic-mineral exports to the US rising even as Japan-bound shipments plunge, an apparent deliberate wedge between the two allies.
sections.whyItMatters: Mineral leverage is being used tactically: China appears to reward the US to strain the US-Japan axis, while pressing Indonesia — the one supplier it does not control — over nickel output. Battery and chip supply chains are now actively weaponized, not just geopolitically exposed.

sections.heading: Iran-Linked Attack on a UK Power Plant Prompts OT Security Warning
sections.body:
Iran-linked hackers knocked a UK power plant offline for four days — described by NY Post and Eastern Herald as the first-ever such cyberattack on a British energy facility. UK officials said the strike did not threaten the wider electrical supply, but it triggered a government briefing to energy chiefs and prompted the NCSC to issue a new warning over operational technology (OT) and edge devices.

Per CyberNews, the hackers have vowed to target US allies as Tehran expands its cyber campaign beyond American critical infrastructure. The attack is part of a pattern alongside the ongoing US disruption of Chinese state-sponsored platforms: the Justice Department and FBI recently announced court-authorized seizures dismantling two Chinese hacking platforms, 'QScan' and 'QTRouter', which had targeted US agencies and critical infrastructure (per Homeland Security Today).
sections.whyItMatters: State-linked attacks are moving down the stack — from IT networks into operational technology that runs physical infrastructure. The UK plant hit shows adversaries can now reach the equipment that keeps lights on, even if they have not yet caused cascading outages.

sections.heading: Nvidia Builds Data Centers, Not Just the Chips
sections.body:
Nvidia is financing land and power for an Ohio campus that OpenAI will lease for 20 years, according to Forbes. TechRepublic reports Nvidia will invest $1.5 billion in SB Energy to help build and operate an eight-gigawatt Ohio data center for OpenAI. The move extends the chipmaker's reach from silicon and software into the physical infrastructure layer.

Relatedly, CNET/SiliconAngle reporting notes an Allianz finding that hyperscalers and large tech providers now absorb roughly two-thirds of all AI spending. Nvidia is also replacing water-evaporating cooling towers with closed-loop liquid systems, removing one of AI data centers' biggest physical expansion bottlenecks — cooling accounts for roughly 40% of a data center's electricity, MSN reports. Meanwhile Forbes details the emerging US effort to close a loophole where advanced chips reach China via cloud access rather than direct shipment.
sections.whyItMatters: Compute power, not just chip supply, has become the binding constraint — and Nvidia is vertically integrating into power and data-center real estate to keep it flowing. Whichever country can marshal electricity at scale will set the pace for frontier AI.

bottomLine: The defining development today is Beijing considering export controls on its own AI models and chips — China positioning itself as the next gatekeeper of AI technology rather than just a consumer of it. That shift, plus state-backed attacks reaching UK operational technology, the hardening US-China race for orbital weapons, and mineral leverage being applied against both Japan and Indonesia, all point to the same conclusion: the tools of the tech-war era — export licensing, orbital hardware, grid infrastructure, and mineral supply — are being consolidated into fewer hands, and Beijing is now playing the same game Washington started.
sources: Financial Times, Reuters, TheNextWeb, Asia Times, Asahi Shimbun, Business Times, MSN, NY Post, Eastern Herald, CyberNews, NCSC, Homeland Security Today, Forbes, TechRepublic, SiliconAngle, Allianz
